lmsArticle.title: Azure Cosmos DB API Modes Explained: NoSQL, MongoDB, Cassandra, PostgreSQL, Gremlin, and Table
lmsArticle.subtitle: What each API can and cannot do — and the compatibility gaps that break production migrations
lmsArticle.excerpt: Cosmos DB's six API modes are wire-protocol compatibility layers over one shared ARS storage engine — except PostgreSQL (Citus), which is genuinely different. Every API emulates its native database incompletely, and those gaps are structural, not bugs. API mode is permanent and cannot be changed after account creation. NoSQL API is the only one with full Cosmos DB feature access. MongoDB API fails silently on complex aggregation pipelines. Cassandra API lacks materialized views and cross-partition transactions. PostgreSQL API is a managed Citus cluster — a different product entirely. Choose the right API before writing the first byte.
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context Cosmos DB's six API modes are wire-protocol compatibility layers over one shared ARS storage engine — except PostgreSQL (Citus), which is genuinely different. Every API emulates its native database incompletely, and those gaps are structural, not bugs. API mode is permanent and cannot be changed after account creation. NoSQL API is the only one with full Cosmos DB feature access. MongoDB API fails silently on comple… This walkthrough focuses on **Cosmos DB's Deceptive Promise: Six APIs, One Underlying Engine**. Before making a design choice, clarify: - A backend team at a mid-sized SaaS company spent three months migrating their MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB using the MongoDB API. - The pitch was compelling: keep your existing MongoDB drivers, point them at a new connection string, and get Azure-managed global distribution and SLAs without any rewrite. - It worked perfectly in staging. **Concepts in play:** database-indexing, btree-vs-lsmtree, consistency-replication, database-sharding ## Stage 1 — Wire-Protocol Translation: How Cosmos DB's API Modes Actually Work - Before diving into individual APIs, it helps to understand the mechanism. - Cosmos DB is not six separate databases that happen to share a cloud control plane. - It is one storage engine with six protocol adapters bolted on top. - The storage engine is called ARS — Atom-Record-Sequence . *Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.* **Observable outcome:** The storage engine is called ARS — Atom-Record-Sequence . ## Stage 2 — The Six API Modes: Capabilities, Scope, and Migration Fit - Each API mode targets a different category of workload and migration scenario. - Here is the ground-level map before the deep-dive on individual gaps. - NoSQL API (formerly Core/SQL API) is Cosmos DB's native interface. - There is no translation layer — ARS speaks this dialect directly. *Applies **btree-vs-lsmtree** to the decision above.* **Observable outcome:** There is no translation layer — ARS speaks this dialect directly. ## Stage 3 — Anatomy of the Compatibility Gaps: Internals and Performance Impact - Understanding where the gaps come from — not just what they are — prevents you from designing workarounds that will also fail. - Internals: How the ARS Engine Creates Structural Gaps ARS manages data as a hierarchy: database → container → logical partition → physical partition . - Every operation in ARS is scoped to a logical partition, identified by the partition key value. - Within a single logical partition, ARS can provide ACID guarantees: reads see a consistent snapshot, writes are ordered, and multi-document transactions commit atomically. *Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.* ```mermaid flowchart TD DB["Database
(WAL/Log)"] Capture["Capture Engine"] Transform["Transform"] Sink["Sink/Destination"] DB -->|"Change Log"| Capture Capture -->|"CDC Event"| Transform Transform -->|"Normalized"| Sink ``` **Observable outcome:** Within a single logical partition, ARS can provide ACID guarantees: reads see a consistent snapshot, writes are ordered, and multi-document transactions commit atomically. ## Stage 4 — The Full Architecture: From Client to Storage Across Every API - The diagram below shows how each API mode sits as a protocol translation layer between the client and the underlying ARS storage engine. - The PostgreSQL API (Citus) is shown separately because it does not share the ARS engine. - The diagram makes the structural split visible. - Five of the six API modes (MongoDB, Cassandra, NoSQL, Gremlin, Table) are protocol adapters routing into the same ARS storage engine — which is why they share the same partition model, the same consistency levels, and t… *Applies **database-sharding** to the decision above.* ```architecture { "version": 1, "title": "The Full Architecture: From Client to Storage Across Every API - Subsystem Overview", "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persistent datastores.", "view": "high-level", "pattern": "microservices", "direction": "LR", "groups": [ { "id": "edge", "label": "Edge Traffic Ingress", "tone": "slate" }, { "id": "services", "label": "Stateless Microservices", "tone": "blue" }, { "id": "data", "label": "Datastore Infrastructure", "tone": "green" } ], "nodes": [ { "id": "gw", "component": "api-gateway", "label": "API Gateway", "group": "edge", "badge": "TLS & Auth" }, { "id": "app", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Domain Service", "group": "services", "badge": "Stateless" }, { "id": "cache", "component": "redis", "label": "Redis Cache", "group": "data", "badge": "Sub-ms Reads" }, { "id": "db", "component": "postgres", "label": "Transactional DB", "group": "data", "badge": "ACID Log" } ], "edges": [ { "from": "gw", "to": "app", "kind": "request", "label": "gRPC Request" }, { "from": "app", "to": "cache", "kind": "read", "label": "Cache Lookups" }, { "from": "app", "to": "db", "kind": "write", "label": "Durable Write" } ], "takeaway": { "title": "Architecture Boundary Invariant", "body": "Stateless compute nodes scale horizontally while shielding underlying database clusters behind fast cache layers." } } ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph Clients A[MongoDB Driver] B[Cassandra Driver / cqlsh] C[Azure SDK / NoSQL SDK] D[Gremlin Client / TinkerPop] E[Azure Table Storage SDK] F[PostgreSQL Client / psql] end subgraph CosmosDB_ARS[Cosmos DB ARS Engine] direction TB M[MongoDB Protocol Adapter] K[Cassandra CQL Adapter] N[NoSQL Native Layer] G[Gremlin TinkerPop Adapter] T[Table OData Adapter] ARS[(ARS Storage Engine Partitioned JSON atoms Multi-region replication 5 consistency levels)] M --> ARS K --> ARS N --> ARS G --> ARS T --> ARS end subgraph CosmosDB_PG[Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL] direction TB PG[PostgreSQL / Citus Distributed query executor Full ACID JOINs Extensions] end A --> M B --> K C --> N D --> G E --> T F --> PG style ARS fill:#1e3a5f,color:#fff style PG fill:#336791,color:#fff style CosmosDB_ARS fill:#0f2540,color:#ccc style CosmosDB_PG fill:#1a3a5c,color:#ccc ``` **Observable outcome:** Five of the six API modes (MongoDB, Cassandra, NoSQL, Gremlin, Table) are protocol adapters routing into the same ARS storage engine — which is why they share the same partition model, the same consistency levels, and t… ## Stage 5 — Where Each API Succeeds and Fails in Production Migrations - Real-world migration outcomes fall into three categories: clean migrations where the API covers all required functionality, conditional migrations where the API works but requires query pattern changes, and blocked migr… - MongoDB API — Conditional for most, blocked for complex aggregation: Teams migrating MongoDB 3.6/4.0 apps that use CRUD and simple aggregation ( $match , $group , $project , $sort , $limit ) consistently report clean mi… - The driver reconnects, basic features work, and RU provisioning replaces ops overhead. - The migration fails when the app uses $lookup across collections, $graphLookup , $facet , $bucket , text search ( $text index), or change streams with precise resume-token semantics. *Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.* **Observable outcome:** The migration fails when the app uses $lookup across collections, $graphLookup , $facet , $bucket , text search ( $text index), or change streams with precise resume-token semantics. ## Stage 6 — The Compatibility Gap Tables: What Each API Cannot Do - These tables cover the gaps that most frequently block or complicate production migrations. - The "Impact" column describes the real consequence teams encounter. - MongoDB API Gaps Cassandra API Gaps Gremlin API Gaps *Applies **btree-vs-lsmtree** to the decision above.* **Observable outcome:** MongoDB API Gaps Cassandra API Gaps Gremlin API Gaps ## End-to-end outcome After working through the stages, you should be able to explain: - The "looks like MongoDB" assumption is the most dangerous. - Teams that evaluate Cosmos DB's MongoDB API by running their basic test suite almost always get a green signal. ## Alternatives considered The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here. ## Failure and degraded modes The source does not isolate a separate failure mode. Limits that matter for the scenario are called out in the stage decisions above.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
seriesList.description: Master the core of computer science. This series demystifies Data Structures and Algorithms, from Big O to graph theory. Learn to write efficient, scalable code and ace your technical interviews with confidence.

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
